title: Planned Obsolescence: Engine of the Consumer Economy
summary: Josh and Chuck explore planned obsolescence, the practice of deliberately making products last a shorter time so consumers buy replacements. They cover its origins in the lightbulb industry (the Phoebus Cartel of the 1920s, the Centennial light), Alfred P. Sloan's dynamic obsolescence at General Motors, Bernard London's 1932 pamphlet "Ending the Depression through Planned Obsolescence," Roy Sheldon and Egmont Arens's "Consumer Engineering," and Brooks Stevens's 1954 speech. They discuss Vance Packard's The Waste Makers, modern examples (Apple's battery throttling and lawsuit, printer ink cartridge chips, auto parts discontinuation and repair control, clothing, textbooks, toys and contrived durability), a German Öko-Institut study on shortened appliance lifespans, e-waste, Europe's Ecodesign Directive, and US right-to-repair bills. The episode closes with a listener mail from Tom about his daughter Grace.
topics: Ending the Depression through Planned Obsolescence

segments.title: Tour dates announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce upcoming tour dates in Toronto, Chicago, Boston, Portland Maine, Orlando, New Orleans and Brooklyn, with tickets via sysk live.

segments.title: Introduction to planned obsolescence
segments.summary: Hosts introduce planned obsolescence, reminisce about durable appliances from childhood, and frame the question of whether the practice is real, deliberate, or simply part of the modern economy.

segments.title: Lightbulbs and the Phoebus Cartel
segments.summary: Edison-era carbon filament bulbs were built to last, and the Centennial light (1901) still burns. The hosts describe the 1920s Phoebus Cartel, in which electric companies and bulb makers colluded to shorten bulb life.

segments.title: Dynamic obsolescence and Alfred Sloan
segments.summary: Alfred P. Sloan of General Motors promoted annual model changes to encourage trade-ins, known as dynamic obsolescence. The hosts discuss the early auto industry.

segments.title: Bernard London's pamphlet and Roy Sheldon and Egmont Arens
segments.summary: Bernard London's 1932 pamphlet proposed artificial expiration dates and taxing consumers who kept products past them. The same year Roy Sheldon and Egmont Arens wrote Consumer Engineering, advocating less durable goods. The hosts note the Depression-era economic motive and discuss vintage appliances.
topics: Ending the Depression through Planned Obsolescence

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of Brooks Stevens.

segments.title: Brooks Stevens and Vance Packard
segments.summary: Milwaukee industrial designer Brooks Stevens's 1954 speech about instilling the desire to own something newer sooner. Vance Packard's 1960 book The Waste Makers followed, and the hosts discuss Packard's other works and a possible short stuff episode.

segments.title: Apple, printers, cars and clothing as examples
segments.summary: Examples of modern planned obsolescence: Apple's throttling update and battery replacement program, incompatible ports and adapters, printer cartridge smart chips, auto parts discontinuation and repair control, used Hummer, and clothing like Levi's wearing out.

segments.title: Textbooks, toys and contrived durability
segments.summary: Hosts discuss college textbook new editions with changed page numbers and contrived durability in toys using inferior parts, plus the decline of repair shops.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Break before the discussion of the problems and statistics.

segments.title: Statistics, e-waste, and regulation
segments.summary: Discussion of a 2015 Öko-Institut study showing rising early replacement of electronics and appliances, customer service, e-waste and recycling rates, Europe's Ecodesign Directive, and US right-to-repair bills. The hosts weigh arguments that obsolescence drives innovation and jobs and close with the open question of which came first.

segments.title: Listener mail from Tom about Grace
segments.summary: Listener Tom writes that the show influenced his daughter Grace, heading to the University of Minnesota, and the family will attend the Chicago show.
